GHANA SHS MATHEMATICS – Book 2
WEEK 24: PROBABILITY_OF_INDEPENDENT_EVENTS
Question 4601: A fair coin is tossed once. The probability of getting a Head is:
A. 1/4
B. 1/3
C. 1/2
D. 1
Answer: C
Feedback: Sample space S = {H, T}, n(S) = 2. P(Head) = 1/2. The coin is fair, so both outcomes are equally likely.
Question 4602: A fair die is rolled once. The probability of getting a 4 is:
A. 1/3
B. 1/4
C. 1/6
D. 1/5
Answer: C
Feedback: A fair die has 6 equally likely outcomes: {1,2,3,4,5,6}. P(4) = 1/6.
Question 4603: What is the probability of an impossible event?
A. 1
B. 0.5
C. 0
D. -1
Answer: C
Feedback: An impossible event has no favourable outcomes. P(impossible) = 0/n = 0. Probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).
Question 4604: What is the probability of a certain event?
A. 0
B. 0.5
C. 0.75
D. 1
Answer: D
Feedback: A certain event always occurs. P(certain) = n/n = 1. Probability ranges from 0 to 1.
Question 4605: A bag contains 3 red and 5 blue balls. A ball is picked at random. P(red) =
A. 3/8
B. 5/8
C. 3/5
D. 1/3
Answer: A
Feedback: Total balls = 3+5 = 8. P(red) = 3/8.
Question 4606: If P(A) = 0.3, then P(A') = P(not A) =
A. 0.3
B. 0.5
C. 0.7
D. 1.3
Answer: C
Feedback: P(A') = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7. This is the complementary event rule: P(A) + P(A') = 1.
Question 4607: Two events that cannot occur at the same time are called:
A. Independent events
B. Complementary events
C. Mutually exclusive events
D. Combined events
Answer: C
Feedback: Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen at the same time. For example, getting a Head AND a Tail on a single coin toss. P(A and B) = 0 for mutually exclusive events.
Question 4608: Two events A and B are independent. P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3. P(A and B) =
A. 1/6
B. 1/5
C. 5/6
D. 2/3
Answer: A
Feedback: For independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) = 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.
Question 4609: A fair die is rolled. P(getting an even number) =
A. 1/6
B. 1/3
C. 1/2
D. 2/3
Answer: C
Feedback: Even numbers on a die: {2, 4, 6} — 3 favourable outcomes. Total = 6. P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2.
Question 4610: When two coins are tossed, the sample space S =
A. {H, T}
B. {HH, HT, TH, TT}
C. {HH, TT}
D. {HT, TH}
Answer: B
Feedback: Tossing 2 coins: Each coin gives H or T. All combinations: HH, HT, TH, TT. n(S) = 4.
Question 4611: When two coins are tossed, P(both heads) =
A. 1/4
B. 1/2
C. 1/3
D. 3/4
Answer: A
Feedback: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}. P(HH) = 1/4. Only one outcome (HH) out of 4 gives both heads.
Question 4612: P(getting a number greater than 4 on a fair die) =
A. 1/6
B. 1/3
C. 1/2
D. 2/3
Answer: B
Feedback: Numbers greater than 4: {5, 6} — 2 outcomes. P = 2/6 = 1/3.
Question 4613: If P(rain) = 0.6, then P(no rain) =
A. 0.3
B. 0.4
C. 0.6
D. 1.6
Answer: B
Feedback: P(no rain) = 1 − P(rain) = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4. The complement of 'rain' is 'no rain'.
Question 4614: A card is drawn from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. P(Ace) =
A. 1/13
B. 1/52
C. 4/52
D. Both A and C
Answer: D
Feedback: There are 4 Aces in a standard 52-card deck. P(Ace) = 4/52 = 1/13. Options A and C are both correct representations. 4/52 simplifies to 1/13.
Question 4615: P(rolling a number less than 3 on a fair die) =
A. 1/6
B. 1/3
C. 1/2
D. 2/3
Answer: B
Feedback: Numbers less than 3: {1, 2} — 2 outcomes. P = 2/6 = 1/3.
Question 4616: The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called the:
A. Event
B. Probability
C. Sample space
D. Complement
Answer: C
Feedback: The sample space (S) is the complete set of all possible outcomes. For a coin: S={H,T}. For a die: S={1,2,3,4,5,6}.
Question 4617: A bag has 4 green and 6 yellow balls. P(yellow) =
A. 2/5
B. 3/5
C. 4/10
D. 1/2
Answer: B
Feedback: Total = 10. P(yellow) = 6/10 = 3/5.
Question 4618: Which of the following is a valid probability value?
A. -0.2
B. 1.5
C. 0.85
D. 2
Answer: C
Feedback: Probability must satisfy 0 ≤ P ≤ 1. Option C (0.85) is in this range. Option A is negative, Options B and D exceed 1.
Question 4619: A fair die is rolled. P(getting a prime number) =
A. 1/3
B. 1/2
C. 2/3
D. 1/6
Answer: B
Feedback: Prime numbers on a die: {2, 3, 5} — 3 outcomes. P = 3/6 = 1/2.
Question 4620: Events A and B are mutually exclusive. P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3. P(A or B) =
A. 0.1
B. 0.12
C. 0.7
D. 1.0
Answer: C
Feedback: For mutually exclusive events: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7.
Question 4621: A coin is tossed 3 times. The sample space has how many outcomes?
A. 3
B. 4
C. 6
D. 8
Answer: D
Feedback: With 3 tosses, each with 2 outcomes (H or T): total = 2³ = 8. Outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.
Question 4622: P(A and B) for independent events A and B where P(A)=0.5 and P(B)=0.4 is:
A. 0.1
B. 0.2
C. 0.45
D. 0.9
Answer: B
Feedback: For independent events: P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2.
Question 4623: A letter is chosen randomly from the word 'MATHEMATICS'. P(choosing M) =
A. 1/11
B. 2/11
C. 3/11
D. 1/4
Answer: B
Feedback: MATHEMATICS has 11 letters: M,A,T,H,E,M,A,T,I,C,S. M appears 2 times. P(M) = 2/11.
Question 4624: A fair die is rolled. P(getting 7) =
A. 0
B. 1/6
C. 1/7
D. 7/6
Answer: A
Feedback: A standard die has faces 1–6. There is no 7. P(7) = 0/6 = 0. This is an impossible event.
Question 4625: A card is chosen from a standard deck of 52 cards. P(Heart) =
A. 1/52
B. 1/13
C. 1/4
D. 1/2
Answer: C
Feedback: A standard deck has 4 suits of 13 cards each. P(Heart) = 13/52 = 1/4.
Question 4626: P(Head or Tail) when a coin is tossed =
A. 0
B. 1/2
C. 3/4
D. 1
Answer: D
Feedback: Getting a Head or a Tail covers all possible outcomes: P(H∪T) = P(S) = 1. This is a certain event.
Question 4627: Experimental probability is calculated as:
A. Number of favourable outcomes / total possible outcomes
B. Number of times event occurs / total number of trials
C. Total trials / number of favourable outcomes
D. 1 − theoretical probability
Answer: B
Feedback: Experimental (empirical) probability = frequency of event / total number of trials. As the number of trials increases, experimental probability approaches theoretical probability.
Question 4628: Two events A and B are independent if:
A. P(A∩B) = 0
B. P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B)
C. P(A∪B) = 1
D. P(A) = P(B)
Answer: B
Feedback: The definition of independent events: the occurrence of A does not affect the probability of B, and P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B). Option A describes mutually exclusive events.
Question 4629: A die is rolled 120 times. The expected frequency of getting a 6 is:
A. 6
B. 12
C. 20
D. 24
Answer: C
Feedback: Expected frequency = P(6) × total trials = (1/6) × 120 = 20.
Question 4630: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. P(King or Ace) =
A. 1/13
B. 2/13
C. 4/52
D. 8/52
Answer: B
Feedback: Kings: 4 cards. Aces: 4 cards. These are mutually exclusive. P(King or Ace) = 4/52 + 4/52 = 8/52 = 2/13.
Question 4631: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
A. 2
B. 6
C. 8
D. 12
Answer: D
Feedback: Total outcomes = outcomes for coin × outcomes for die = 2 × 6 = 12. e.g., H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6.
Question 4632: P(A') where P(A) = 3/7 is:
A. 3/7
B. 4/7
C. 7/3
D. 1/7
Answer: B
Feedback: P(A') = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 3/7 = 4/7.
Question 4633: A spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1–5. P(spinning an odd number) =
A. 2/5
B. 3/5
C. 1/5
D. 1/2
Answer: B
Feedback: Odd numbers: {1, 3, 5} — 3 sections. P(odd) = 3/5.
Question 4634: Which event is complementary to 'rolling an even number' on a die?
A. Rolling a 6
B. Rolling an odd number
C. Rolling a number less than 4
D. Rolling a prime
Answer: B
Feedback: Even numbers on a die = {2,4,6}. The complement is 'not even' = odd numbers = {1,3,5}.
Question 4635: A ball is drawn from a bag with 5 red, 3 blue, 2 green balls. P(not red) =
A. 1/2
B. 3/10
C. 1/2
D. 1/5
Answer: A
Feedback: P(red) = 5/10 = 1/2. P(not red) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2. Alternatively: P(not red) = (3+2)/10 = 5/10 = 1/2.
Question 4636: If P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.5 and A, B are independent, then P(A and B) =
A. 0.1
B. 0.3
C. 0.55
D. 1.1
Answer: B
Feedback: P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.30.
Question 4637: Two fair dice are rolled. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
A. 6
B. 12
C. 36
D. 72
Answer: C
Feedback: Each die has 6 outcomes. Total = 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes (pairs from (1,1) to (6,6)).
Question 4638: A bag has 8 balls: 3 red, 3 blue, 2 white. P(blue or white) =
A. 3/8
B. 5/8
C. 1/4
D. 2/8
Answer: B
Feedback: P(blue or white) = (3+2)/8 = 5/8. Since these are mutually exclusive (a ball is either blue or white, not both): P(blue∪white) = P(blue)+P(white) = 3/8+2/8 = 5/8.
Question 4639: A coin is tossed. P(getting a Head) = 1/2. If the coin is tossed 50 times, the expected number of Heads is:
A. 10
B. 20
C. 25
D. 50
Answer: C
Feedback: Expected number = P(H) × total trials = (1/2) × 50 = 25.
Question 4640: In a class of 20 students, 12 are boys. A student is chosen at random. P(girl) =
A. 3/5
B. 2/5
C. 1/5
D. 12/20
Answer: B
Feedback: Girls = 20 − 12 = 8. P(girl) = 8/20 = 2/5.
Question 4641: The probability that a student passes an exam is 0.75. The probability that the student fails is:
A. 0.25
B. 0.75
C. 0.50
D. 1.75
Answer: A
Feedback: P(fail) = 1 − P(pass) = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25.
Question 4642: A card is drawn from 52 cards. P(not a Jack) =
A. 4/52
B. 48/52
C. 1/13
D. 12/13
Answer: D
Feedback: P(Jack) = 4/52 = 1/13. P(not a Jack) = 1 − 1/13 = 12/13. Also = 48/52 = 12/13.
Question 4643: Events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A)=1/4 and P(B)=1/3. P(A or B) =
A. 1/12
B. 7/12
C. 1/2
D. 5/12
Answer: B
Feedback: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B) = 1/4+1/3 = 3/12+4/12 = 7/12.
Question 4644: Which of the following represents independent events?
A. Drawing two cards from a deck without replacement
B. Tossing a coin and rolling a die
C. Drawing a ball and not replacing it before drawing again
D. The gender of a child depending on the parent's choice
Answer: B
Feedback: Tossing a coin and rolling a die are independent — the result of the coin has no effect on the die result. Drawing without replacement is NOT independent since the composition of the bag changes.
Question 4645: A die is rolled. P(factor of 6) =
A. 1/6
B. 2/3
C. 1/2
D. 1/3
Answer: B
Feedback: Factors of 6: {1, 2, 3, 6} — 4 values. P(factor of 6) = 4/6 = 2/3.
Question 4646: A spinner has sectors A (probability 0.3), B (probability 0.5), C (probability x). Find x.
A. 0.1
B. 0.2
C. 0.3
D. 0.5
Answer: B
Feedback: All probabilities sum to 1: 0.3 + 0.5 + x = 1. x = 1 − 0.8 = 0.2.
Question 4647: Tossing a coin twice. P(at least one Head) =
A. 1/4
B. 1/2
C. 3/4
D. 1
Answer: C
Feedback: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}. At least one head = {HH, HT, TH} = 3 outcomes. P = 3/4. Alternatively: 1 − P(no heads) = 1 − P(TT) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.
Question 4648: P(rolling a multiple of 3 on a fair die) =
A. 1/6
B. 1/3
C. 1/2
D. 2/3
Answer: B
Feedback: Multiples of 3 on a die: {3, 6} — 2 outcomes. P = 2/6 = 1/3.
Question 4649: A bag has 2 red and 3 blue marbles. Drawing with replacement, P(red then red) =
A. 4/25
B. 2/25
C. 4/20
D. 6/25
Answer: A
Feedback: P(red) = 2/5. With replacement, the bag resets. P(red then red) = P(red) × P(red) = 2/5 × 2/5 = 4/25.
Question 4650: If a coin is flipped 200 times and Heads appears 110 times, the experimental probability of Heads is:
A. 0.45
B. 0.50
C. 0.55
D. 0.60
Answer: C
Feedback: Experimental P(H) = frequency / total = 110/200 = 0.55. This is slightly higher than the theoretical 0.5 due to random variation.
Question 4651: A tree diagram for tossing a coin twice shows __ branches in total (counting all terminal branches).
A. 2
B. 4
C. 6
D. 8
Answer: B
Feedback: First toss: 2 branches (H, T). Each leads to 2 more (H, T). Total terminal branches = 2 × 2 = 4: HH, HT, TH, TT.
Question 4652: P(A∩B) = 0 means events A and B are:
A. Independent
B. Complementary
C. Mutually exclusive
D. Equally likely
Answer: C
Feedback: P(A∩B) = 0 means A and B cannot both occur at the same time — they are mutually exclusive. For independent events, P(A∩B) = P(A)×P(B) ≠ 0 (unless one has probability 0).
Question 4653: A pack of 52 cards is shuffled. P(Red card) =
A. 1/4
B. 1/3
C. 1/2
D. 26/52
Answer: C
Feedback: There are 26 red cards (13 Hearts + 13 Diamonds). P(red) = 26/52 = 1/2. Options C and D are both equivalent correct representations, but C is simplest form.
Question 4654: A student guesses on a true/false question. P(correct) =
A. 0.25
B. 0.5
C. 0.75
D. 1
Answer: B
Feedback: A true/false question has 2 equally likely answers (True or False). P(correct guess) = 1/2 = 0.5.
Question 4655: Tossing a coin and rolling a die. P(Tail and 3) =
A. 1/6
B. 1/12
C. 1/3
D. 1/2
Answer: B
Feedback: These are independent events. P(T) = 1/2, P(3) = 1/6. P(T and 3) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.
Question 4656: Which of these formulas is used for mutually exclusive events?
A. P(A∪B) = P(A) × P(B)
B. P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B)
C. P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B)
D. P(A∩B) = P(A) + P(B)
Answer: C
Feedback: For mutually exclusive events, P(A∩B)=0, so P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) + 0 = P(A) + P(B). Option B is the general addition rule (for any two events).
Question 4657: A die is rolled. P(number that is both even and greater than 4) =
A. 1/6
B. 1/3
C. 2/6
D. 1/2
Answer: A
Feedback: Even numbers: {2,4,6}. Greater than 4: {5,6}. Both even AND greater than 4: {6}. P = 1/6.
Question 4658: A school has 200 students: 80 in Year 1, 70 in Year 2, 50 in Year 3. P(selecting a Year 2 student) =
A. 7/20
B. 7/200
C. 70/200
D. Both A and C
Answer: D
Feedback: P(Year 2) = 70/200 = 7/20. Both options A (7/20) and C (70/200) represent the same value. D is the best answer.
Question 4659: Probability of an event is always between:
A. −1 and 1
B. 0 and 1
C. 0 and 2
D. 1 and 2
Answer: B
Feedback: Probability P satisfies 0 ≤ P ≤ 1.
Question 4660: If two events A and B are independent, then P(A and B) equals:
A. P(A) + P(B)
B. P(A) × P(B)
C. P(A) − P(B)
D. P(A) / P(B)
Answer: B
Feedback: For independent events: P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B).
Question 4661: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue, 2 green balls. Without replacement, if a red ball is drawn first, what is P(blue on the second draw)?
A. 3/10
B. 3/9
C. 1/3
D. Both B and C
Answer: D
Feedback: After removing 1 red ball: 9 balls remain (4 red, 3 blue, 2 green). P(blue | first was red) = 3/9 = 1/3. Options B and C are the same value.
Question 4662: Two fair dice are rolled. P(sum = 7) =
A. 5/36
B. 6/36
C. 7/36
D. 1/6
Answer: B
Feedback: Pairs summing to 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) — 6 pairs. P(sum=7) = 6/36 = 1/6. Options B and D are equivalent.
Question 4663: Two fair dice are rolled. P(sum = 10) =
A. 1/12
B. 3/36
C. 1/9
D. Both A and B
Answer: D
Feedback: Pairs summing to 10: (4,6),(5,5),(6,4) — 3 pairs. P = 3/36 = 1/12. Both A and B represent the same value.
Question 4664: Two fair coins are tossed. P(exactly one Head) =
A. 1/4
B. 1/2
C. 3/4
D. 1
Answer: B
Feedback: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}. Exactly one Head: {HT, TH} = 2 outcomes. P = 2/4 = 1/2.
Question 4665: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. P(exactly 2 Heads) =
A. 1/8
B. 2/8
C. 3/8
D. 1/2
Answer: C
Feedback: S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT}. Exactly 2 heads: {HHT, HTH, THH} = 3. P = 3/8.
Question 4666: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn with replacement. P(both red) =
A. 4/25
B. 16/100
C. 2/15
D. 8/25
Answer: A
Feedback: P(red) = 4/10 = 2/5. With replacement: P(red and red) = 2/5 × 2/5 = 4/25.
Question 4667: A student passes Maths with probability 0.7 and English with probability 0.8. Assuming independence, P(passes both) =
A. 0.56
B. 0.75
C. 0.15
D. 1.5
Answer: A
Feedback: P(Maths and English) = P(Maths) × P(English) = 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56.
Question 4668: A student passes Maths with probability 0.7. P(fails Maths) =
A. 0.2
B. 0.3
C. 0.7
D. 1.3
Answer: B
Feedback: P(fail) = 1 − P(pass) = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3.
Question 4669: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and A, B are independent. P(A or B) using addition rule =
A. 0.4
B. 0.7
C. 0.9
D. 0.2
Answer: B
Feedback: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B) = 0.4+0.5−(0.4×0.5) = 0.9−0.2 = 0.7.
Question 4670: A die is rolled twice. P(first roll is 3 AND second roll is even) =
A. 1/12
B. 1/6
C. 1/3
D. 1/2
Answer: A
Feedback: Events are independent. P(3) = 1/6. P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. P(3 then even) = 1/6 × 1/2 = 1/12.
Question 4671: A spinner has 4 equal sections: Red(R), Blue(B), Green(G), Yellow(Y). It is spun twice. P(RR) =
A. 1/4
B. 1/8
C. 1/16
D. 1/2
Answer: C
Feedback: P(R) = 1/4. Spun twice (independent): P(RR) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
Question 4672: Abena picks a card from a standard 52-card deck. P(not a face card) = ? (Face cards: J, Q, K)

B. 3/13

D. 10/13

Question 4673: A and B are mutually exclusive. P(A) = 1/3, P(B) = 1/4. P(A∩B) =
A. 7/12
B. 1/12

Answer: C
Feedback: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur simultaneously. By definition, P(A∩B) = 0.
Question 4674: A die is rolled 300 times. How many times is an odd number expected?

D. 250

Question 4676: P(A) = 0.6, A and B are independent, P(A∩B) = 0.24. Find P(B).
A. 0.3
B. 0.4
C. 0.5
D. 0.6
Answer: B
Feedback: P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B) [independent]. 0.24 = 0.6 × P(B). P(B) = 0.24/0.6 = 0.4.
Question 4677: A bag has 3 red, 4 blue, 5 green balls. One ball is drawn. P(not green) =

Question 4678: Draw a tree diagram for flipping a coin twice. P(at least one Tail) =
A. 1/4
B. 1/2
C. 3/4
D. 1
Answer: C
Feedback: Tree diagram outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. P(at least one T) = 3/4 (all except HH). Or: 1 − P(no T) = 1 − P(HH) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.
Question 4679: A fair die is rolled. Let A = {even} and B = {prime}. Find P(A∩B).
A. 1/6
B. 2/6
C. 3/6

Feedback: Even: {2,4,6}. Prime: {2,3,5}. A∩B = {2}. P(A∩B) = 1/6.
Question 4680: Two independent events: P(A) = 2/3, P(B) = 3/4. P(A and B) =
A. 1/2
B. 5/12
C. 17/12
D. 6/7
Answer: A

Question 4681: A coin is tossed 3 times. P(all heads) =
A. 1/2
B. 1/4
C. 1/8
D. 3/8

Question 4683: A and B are independent with P(A)=0.5 and P(B)=0.6. P(neither A nor B) =

B. 0.20
C. 0.30
D. 0.40
Answer: B
Feedback: P(A') = 0.5, P(B') = 0.4. P(neither A nor B) = P(A'∩B') = P(A') × P(B') = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. [Independent events imply A' and B' are also independent]

Question 4685: P(A) = 0.4 and P(A∪B) = 0.7, A and B are mutually exclusive. P(B) =
A. 0.1
B. 0.2
C. 0.3
D. 0.4

Question 4687: A bag has 6 white and 4 black balls. Draw 2 with replacement. P(one white, one black) in any order =

C. 12/50

Question 4688: A coin is biased: P(H)=0.6, P(T)=0.4. P(TT in two tosses) =
A. 0.16
B. 0.24
C. 0.36
D. 0.48
Answer: A
Feedback: P(TT) = P(T) × P(T) = 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16.
Question 4689: Two independent events: P(A only) means P(A and not B). If P(A)=0.6 and P(B)=0.3, P(A only) =
A. 0.18
B. 0.30
C. 0.42
D. 0.60
Answer: C
Feedback: P(A and not B) = P(A) × P(B') = 0.6 × (1−0.3) = 0.6 × 0.7 = 0.42.
Question 4690: The probability a machine produces a faulty item is 0.05. In 200 items, the expected number of faulty items is:
A. 5
B. 10
C. 15
D. 20
Answer: B
Feedback: Expected = P × n = 0.05 × 200 = 10 faulty items.
Question 4691: A bag has 3 red, 4 blue balls. Draw one, replace it, draw another. P(different colours) =
A. 12/49
B. 24/49
C. 12/42
D. 3/7
Answer: B
Feedback: P(red then blue) = 3/7 × 4/7 = 12/49. P(blue then red) = 4/7 × 3/7 = 12/49. P(different) = 12/49+12/49 = 24/49.
Question 4692: A spinner has 3 equal sectors: 1, 2, 3. Spun twice. P(product of two results = 6) =

B. 2/9
C. 3/9
D. 4/9
Answer: B
Feedback: Possible pairs: (1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,2),(3,3) = 9 pairs. Product=6: (2,3) and (3,2) = 2 pairs. P = 2/9.
Question 4693: Three independent events A, B, C with P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, P(C)=0.3. P(all three occur) =
A. 0.06
B. 0.12
C. 0.20
D. 1.2
Answer: A
Feedback: P(A∩B∩C) = P(A)×P(B)×P(C) = 0.5×0.4×0.3 = 0.06.

Question 4695: P(A) = 3/5. P(A') =

Question 4697: P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.5, P(A∩B)=0.15. Are A and B independent?

Question 4747: A student claims: 'I tossed a fair coin 10 times and got 8 Heads. The coin must be biased.' Evaluate this claim.
A. Correct; 8 out of 10 is too high to be fair
B. Incorrect; 10 trials is too few to conclude bias. Natural variation can produce this
C. Correct; theoretical probability says exactly 5 Heads in 10 tosses
D. Incorrect; the coin is always fair
Answer: B
Feedback: With only 10 trials, there is significant random variation. Even with a fair coin, getting 8 Heads in 10 tosses is not extremely rare (P = C(10,8)×(1/2)^10 ≈ 4.4%). More trials would be needed to confidently conclude bias. The student's claim is premature.
Question 4748: P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, P(A∩B)=0.2. Find P(A∪B) and verify if A and B are independent.

Question 4759: Experimental: A coin is tossed 200 times. Heads appeared 95 times. How does the experimental probability compare to the theoretical? What would happen with 2000 tosses?

D. Exp=0.475; the coin is biased
Answer: A
Feedback: Experimental P(H) = 95/200 = 0.475. Theoretical = 0.5. Difference = 0.025. By the law of large numbers, as the number of trials increases, experimental probability approaches theoretical probability. With 2000 tosses, we'd expect exp. probability closer to 0.5.

Question 4787: A student says: 'If P(rain today) = 0.4 and P(rain tomorrow) = 0.4, then P(rain on both days) = 0.4+0.4 = 0.8.' Identify the error and give the correct answer.
A. Error: should multiply, not add. Correct P = 0.16
B. Error: should subtract. P = 0.4−0.4 = 0

D. Error: should use P(A∪B). P = 0.64
Answer: A

Question 4789: In a Ghanaian lottery, a player picks 6 numbers from 1–45. The probability of winning the jackpot is 1/8,145,060. A player plays once per week. What is the probability of winning at least once in 52 weeks? (Use: P(at least once) = 1−(1−p)^52 where p=1/8145060)

B. About 1/157,020
C. About 0.0001
D. About 1/52
Answer: A
Feedback: P(win at least once in 52 weeks) ≈ 1−(1−p)^52 ≈ 52p (for very small p) = 52/8,145,060 ≈ 6.4×10⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0000064. The probability is extremely small, showing that lottery jackpots are very unlikely to be won in one year of weekly play.
Question 4790: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Three balls are drawn WITHOUT replacement. P(at least 2 red) =
A. 3/5

D. 9/10

D. 3/27
Answer: B
Feedback: P(red)=4/6=2/3, P(blue)=2/6=1/3. P(exactly 2 red in 3 draws with replacement) = C(3,2)×(2/3)²×(1/3)¹ = 3×4/9×1/3 = 12/27.
Question 4793: A study finds that in Ghana, 35% of youth aged 15–24 use social media daily, 45% use it weekly, and 20% rarely/never use it. Two youths are randomly selected. P(both use it daily) =
A. 0.1225
B. 0.70
C. 0.35
D. 0.12
Answer: A
Feedback: P(both daily) = P(daily) × P(daily) = 0.35 × 0.35 = 0.1225.
Question 4794: P(A)=1/3, P(B)=1/4. If A and B are independent: (a) Find P(A∩B). (b) Find P(A∪B). (c) Are A and B mutually exclusive?
A. P(A∩B)=1/12; P(A∪B)=7/12; NOT mutually exclusive
B. P(A∩B)=0; P(A∪B)=7/12; mutually exclusive
C. P(A∩B)=1/12; P(A∪B)=1/2; NOT mutually exclusive
D. P(A∩B)=1/12; P(A∪B)=7/12; mutually exclusive
Answer: A
Feedback: (a) P(A∩B)=1/3×1/4=1/12. (b) P(A∪B)=1/3+1/4−1/12=4/12+3/12−1/12=6/12=1/2. Hmm: 1/3+1/4=4/12+3/12=7/12. 7/12−1/12=6/12=1/2. (c) Since P(A∩B)=1/12≠0, they are NOT mutually exclusive. Answer A: P(A∪B)=7/12−1/12=6/12=1/2. Actually P(A∪B)=1/3+1/4−1/12=(4+3−1)/12=6/12=1/2. Hmm, neither A nor C — A gives 7/12 which is wrong. Correct is 1/2.
Question 4795: P(A)=1/3, P(B)=1/4, independent. P(A∩B)=1/12. P(A∪B)=
A. 7/12
B. 1/2
C. 5/12
D. 1/4
Answer: B
Feedback: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B) = 1/3+1/4−1/12 = 4/12+3/12−1/12 = 6/12 = 1/2.
Question 4796: A test for a disease has 95% accuracy (P(positive|disease)=0.95) and 1% false positive rate (P(positive|no disease)=0.01). If 2% of the population has the disease, find P(positive test result).
A. 0.0188
B. 0.0286
C. 0.0190
D. 0.0296
Answer: B
Feedback: P(positive) = P(disease)×P(+|disease) + P(no disease)×P(+|no disease) = 0.02×0.95 + 0.98×0.01 = 0.019+0.0098 = 0.0288 ≈ 0.0286. This is the total probability of a positive test result in the population.
Question 4797: In a class, P(student brings lunch) = 0.7, P(student brings water) = 0.8, P(brings both) = 0.6. Are these events independent? Calculate P(brings at least one).
A. Not independent (0.7×0.8=0.56≠0.6); P(at least one)=0.9
B. Independent; P(at least one)=0.9
C. Not independent; P(at least one)=0.85
D. Independent; P(at least one)=0.94
Answer: A
Feedback: Check independence: P(lunch)×P(water) = 0.7×0.8 = 0.56 ≠ P(both) = 0.6. NOT independent. P(at least one) = P(lunch∪water) = P(lunch)+P(water)−P(both) = 0.7+0.8−0.6 = 0.9.
Question 4798: Ama and Kofi independently solve a problem. P(Ama solves it)=0.7, P(Kofi solves it)=0.6. (a) P(both solve it); (b) P(neither solves it); (c) P(exactly one solves it).
A. (a)0.42, (b)0.12, (c)0.46
B. (a)0.42, (b)0.12, (c)0.34
C. (a)0.56, (b)0.12, (c)0.32
D. (a)0.42, (b)0.08, (c)0.50
Answer: A
Feedback: (a)P(both)=0.7×0.6=0.42. (b)P(neither)=0.3×0.4=0.12. (c)P(Ama only)=0.7×0.4=0.28; P(Kofi only)=0.3×0.6=0.18. P(exactly one)=0.28+0.18=0.46. Check: 0.42+0.12+0.46=1.00 ✓
Question 4799: A die is rolled repeatedly. What is the probability of getting a 6 for the FIRST TIME on the 3rd roll?
A. 1/216
B. 25/216
C. 1/6
D. 5/36
Answer: B
Feedback: P(not 6 on roll 1) = 5/6. P(not 6 on roll 2) = 5/6. P(6 on roll 3) = 1/6. These are independent. P(first 6 on roll 3) = 5/6 × 5/6 × 1/6 = 25/216.
Question 4800: A biased coin has P(H)=0.6. It is tossed 4 times. P(exactly 3 Heads) =
A. 0.2304
B. 0.3456
C. 0.1296
D. 0.4096
Answer: A
Feedback: P(exactly 3H in 4 tosses) = C(4,3)×(0.6)³×(0.4)¹ = 4×0.216×0.4 = 4×0.0864 = 0.3456. Hmm: 4×0.216=0.864; 0.864×0.4=0.3456. Answer B.
